run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_218 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Two read-only SQL questions were answered from the configured MySQL target 'otel-demo' (schema testdb). The database lists exactly two tables: holmes_eval_218 and orders. The verification code stored in holmes_eval_218 is HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2 (single row, id=1, category=eval_test, created_at 2026-11-21T08:33:01). For the slow-query question, the structural finding is that orders carries only a PRIMARY index on id and no index on customer_id, so EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the optimizer performing a full Table scan on orders (cost=101, rows=1000) and then filtering on orders.customer_id = 12345. On this snapshot the scan of 1000 rows completed in about 0.42 ms, so the reported slowness was NOT reproduced here; the observed fact is the scan plan, while 'the missing index makes this query slow at production scale' remains a hypothesis. Note also that customer_id values in this table span 1..999, so the literal 12345 matches zero rows in this dataset.

claims.text: The configured MySQL database (dialect mysql, schema testdb, target otel-demo) contains exactly two tables: holmes_eval_218 and orders.
Table holmes_eval_218 has columns id (int, primary key), category (varchar(50)), verification_code (varchar(100)) and created_at (timestamp, default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP).

holmes_eval_218 holds one row returned at query time: id=1, category='eval_test', verification_code='HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2', created_at='2026-11-21T08:33:01'. That value is the verification code.

Table orders has columns id (int, not null), customer_id (int, not null), order_date (date, not null), total_amount (decimal(10,2), not null), status (varchar(20), not null); the only index reported is PRIMARY on id.
information_schema.STATISTICS for testdb.orders returns a single index entry: INDEX_NAME=PRIMARY, COLUMN_NAME=id, NON_UNIQUE=0, SEQ_IN_INDEX=1 — there is no index whose leading column is customer_id.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE of 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' returns: '-> Filter: (orders.customer_id = 12345) (cost=101 rows=100) (actual time=0.418..0.418 rows=0 loops=1)' over '-> Table scan on orders (cost=101 rows=1000) (actual time=0.0534..0.368 rows=1000 loops=1)'; the access path is a full table scan followed by a filter.

On this snapshot the statement was not slow: the measured execution of the full table scan plus filter was about 0.42 ms total (rows=1000 scanned, rows=0 returned), so the reported 'slow query' symptom is not reproduced against this 1000-row table.
orders currently contains 1000 rows with 635 distinct customer_id values (about 1.6 rows per customer), i.e. a customer_id predicate would be highly selective if indexed.

customer_id values in orders span min_id=1, max_id=999 (avg 504.1290), so the literal 12345 does not exist in this table and the query legitimately returns 0 rows (COUNT(*) for customer_id = 12345 is 0).
Both tables use InnoDB; orders reports INDEX_LENGTH=0 with DATA_LENGTH=81920 (TABLE_ROWS=1000, AVG_ROW_LENGTH=81), and holmes_eval_218 reports INDEX_LENGTH=0 with DATA_LENGTH=16384 (TABLE_ROWS=1).

Candidate cause of the reported slowness: the absence of any index on orders.customer_id forces a full table scan (O(number of rows)) for every equality lookup, so cost grows linearly with table size; at production row counts the same statement would read the whole table instead of ~1-2 rows per customer. The observed plan supports the mechanism, but the latency growth itself was not observed on this 1000-row snapshot.

Secondary candidate cause, not yet quantified: 'SELECT *' projects and transfers all five columns, including the decimal(10,2) total_amount and varchar(20) status, for every matching row; with many rows per customer or over a network, this adds transfer and row-materialization cost even though the examined plan shows no sorting or temporary table.

Rejected: implicit type conversion or a function/expression applied to customer_id as the reason the index is unusable. customer_id is declared int not null and the plan shows a plain Filter predicate 'orders.customer_id = 12345' with no conversion or wrapping expression — the index is not bypassed by a type mismatch, it simply does not exist.

Advisory fix to validate on a non-production copy: add index CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id); optionally a covering composite (customer_id, order_date) if queries also filter or sort by date. Confirmation would be an EXPLAIN showing an index lookup/range access on orders instead of 'Table scan on orders'.

Advisory: replace 'SELECT *' with the specific columns actually consumed by the caller, and confirm the literal customer_id value (12345 yields no rows in this dataset, so any slowness experienced by a caller cannot come from returning many rows for that value here).

gaps: The reported slow-query latency was not reproduced: the measured EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution on this snapshot was ~0.42 ms over 1000 rows, so the duration the user actually observed (and on which table/dataset) is unknown.
The real orders dataset size is unknown here; the analyzed table holds only 1000 rows, so scan cost at production row counts cannot be measured from this data.
No MySQL query-latency or slow-query-log series were located or queried among the available Prometheus metrics, so there is no time-based evidence of query latency degradation or when it started.
The change_history integration is not available in this Run, so no evidence exists about when the orders table or its indexes were last altered (for example a dropped index).
It is unknown whether customer_id=12345 exists in the customer's production data; in this testdb snapshot customer_id values only span 1..999, so zero rows are returned.
next_steps: Run EXPLAIN (and EXPLAIN ANALYZE) of the same statement against the production-sized dataset to confirm the full-scan plan and measure real cost before and after adding an index.
Have a DBA review and schedule CREATE INDEX on orders(customer_id) (or a composite including order_date) during a low-traffic window; verify with EXPLAIN that the plan switches to an index lookup.

If evidence of an actual incident is needed, pull MySQL slow-query log / performance_schema statements_summary for this statement, since no such telemetry is currently registered in the available metric sources.
Confirm with the application owner whether 'SELECT *' is required, and narrow the projection to the columns used.
